title: How a Stem-Cell Pool Persists While Its Clones Come and Go

scenes.tts: A mouse replaces its intestinal lining every few days. How can its stem-cell supply last when individual clones can vanish? Watch one crypt, the pocket where new lining cells begin.
scenes.visual: Open immediately on one large schematic cutaway of a mouse small-intestinal crypt filling at least 70% of frame height. A handful of blue cartoon cells gently jostle at its rounded base while grey daughter cells stream upward and one exits the top. The gold question appears beside the same crypt. Keep a small full-opacity label, 'simplified schematic', on screen; the upward stream never freezes.
scenes.narration: A mouse replaces its intestinal lining every few days. How can its stem-cell supply last when individual clones can vanish? Watch one crypt, the pocket where new lining cells begin.

scenes.visual: Keep the crypt moving. Briefly place the title 'How a Stem-Cell Pool Persists While Its Clones Come and Go' above it, then shrink the title into a small corner label without cutting away.

scenes.tts: In this simplified picture, a handful of blue stem cells occupy the crypt base. The epithelium is the intestinal lining. Cells need niche contact or signals to keep a base position.
scenes.visual: In the carried crypt, five blue cells occupy visibly outlined but unnumbered schematic positions. Grey daughters flow upward, change into three simple epithelial silhouettes and leave. Add a soft signal glow only around the base, labelled 'niche support'. Keep 'simplified schematic' visible.
scenes.narration: In this simplified picture, a handful of blue stem cells occupy the crypt base. The epithelium is the intestinal lining. Cells need niche contact or signals to keep a base position.

scenes.tts: Stem cells have two jobs. First, they make specialized descendants that leave the base. Second, they maintain a stem-cell pool over time. Neighbours can fill positions as cells leave, so the pool may persist without preserving every cell.
scenes.visual: Outline the schematic base positions with a teal bracket labelled 'stem-cell pool'. Briefly highlight the upward grey output for job one, then transform that highlight into the continuing blue base pool for job two. Let one base cell leave and a neighbour slide into the gap; show no numeric counter.
scenes.narration: Stem cells have two jobs. First, they make specialized descendants that leave the base. Second, they maintain a stem-cell pool over time. Neighbours can fill positions as cells leave, so the pool may persist without preserving every cell.

scenes.tts: Shape or L G R five expression alone cannot prove those jobs. Scientists give one expressing cell a permanent green lineage mark. Every daughter inherits green, even after it stops expressing L G R five. The mark follows ancestry.
scenes.caption: Shape or Lgr5 expression alone cannot prove those jobs. Scientists give one expressing cell a permanent green lineage mark. Every daughter inherits green, even after it stops expressing Lgr5. The mark follows ancestry.
scenes.visual: Keep the same crypt. A yellow tamoxifen pulse sweeps across one blue base cell; that cell turns green. Its small 'Lgr5 now' tag fades as it divides, but both daughters remain green. One green daughter stays at the base and another moves upward. Transform the faded expression tag into a green family-line brace labelled 'ancestry'.
scenes.narration: Shape or Lgr5 expression alone cannot prove those jobs. Scientists give one expressing cell a permanent green lineage mark. Every daughter inherits green, even after it stops expressing Lgr5. The mark follows ancestry.

scenes.tts: Suppose the marked cell is only a short-lived precursor, a cell with limited output. What should happen to green after its descendants leave the lining?
scenes.visual: Split only the time outcome beside the carried crypt, not the world itself. Show a ghosted short green patch rising toward the top, then hold it. Place the gold question in large text above the crypt and a simple time arrow from 'now' to 'later'.
scenes.narration: Suppose the marked cell is only a short-lived precursor, a cell with limited output. What should happen to green after its descendants leave the lining?

scenes.visual: Hold the gold question and the same crypt for thinking time. The grey lining continues a very slow upward drift while the ghosted green patch approaches the top. No new labels appear.

scenes.tts: A short-lived clone would fade away. Instead, observed green ribbons persisted for sixty days and contained every epithelial lineage. A lineage is a descendant family. That is multipotent output: several cell types within one tissue.
scenes.visual: First let the ghosted short patch leave and vanish under a red 'short-lived' label. Then rewind the same crypt and grow a continuous green ribbon from base to top as a time marker advances to '60 days'. Transform cells within the ribbon into labelled absorptive, goblet and enteroendocrine cartoons, plus a labelled Paneth cell at the crypt base. Mark the animation 'schematic reconstruction'.
scenes.narration: A short-lived clone would fade away. Instead, observed green ribbons persisted for sixty days and contained every epithelial lineage. A lineage is a descendant family. That is multipotent output: several cell types within one tissue.

scenes.tts: But a long-lived ribbon does not mean its first green cell survives forever. The trace identifies a stem-cell population through descendant output over time. What descendants do, not a marker alone, supplies the evidence.
scenes.visual: Keep the green ribbon. Fade the original-cell halo while new green descendants replace one another at the base. Move a brace from the single cell to the whole green lineage, changing the label from 'starting cell' to 'population tested over time'. Cross out a small 'marker alone' card in red.
scenes.narration: But a long-lived ribbon does not mean its first green cell survives forever. The trace identifies a stem-cell population through descendant output over time. What descendants do, not a marker alone, supplies the evidence.

scenes.tts: Now give nearby stem cells permanent Confetti colours: green, yellow, red and cyan. In normally renewing mouse small intestine, L G R five-high cells divide about once daily. Most divisions are symmetric. Here that means both daughters retain stem positions, or both leave them.
scenes.caption: Now give nearby stem cells permanent Confetti colours: green, yellow, red and cyan. In normally renewing mouse small intestine, Lgr5-high cells divide about once daily. Most divisions are symmetric. Here that means both daughters retain stem positions, or both leave them.
scenes.visual: Transform the schematic base cells into green, yellow, red and cyan Confetti clones, with one colour repeated. Show one coloured cell making two equal-sized daughters that both remain briefly; then show another division whose daughters move out while a neighbour fills the gap. A small clock turns beside 'about once daily'. Keep 'simplified schematic' visible.
scenes.narration: Now give nearby stem cells permanent Confetti colours: green, yellow, red and cyan. In normally renewing mouse small intestine, Lgr5-high cells divide about once daily. Most divisions are symmetric. Here that means both daughters retain stem positions, or both leave them.

scenes.tts: The clones appear to compete for niche-supported positions. Green expands when red leaves. Red disappears. Later, cyan pushes into green positions. Colour shares change while the total pool stays constrained.
scenes.visual: Run that exact sequence in the carried schematic: a red cell exits, green copies into its position, then cyan later displaces green. Keep the teal pool bracket unchanged. Add a small spinner labelled 'chance' before each replacement; do not imply measured timing.
scenes.narration: The clones appear to compete for niche-supported positions. Green expands when red leaves. Red disappears. Later, cyan pushes into green positions. Colour shares change while the total pool stays constrained.

scenes.tts: Repeated replacements erase most colours and expand another until one clone fills the base. Different repeats produce different winners. The result is takeover by one clone, not survival of every starting clone.
scenes.visual: Continue in the same crypt until yellow spreads across every schematic base position. Then rewind into three small outcome strips beside the large crypt, each ending with a different winning colour. Keep the gold 'chance' spinner turning slowly.
scenes.narration: Repeated replacements erase most colours and expand another until one clone fills the base. Different repeats produce different winners. The result is takeover by one clone, not survival of every starting clone.

scenes.tts: The number of supported positions stays roughly constrained while clone identities change. Balance belongs to the population, not every division. No cell is appointed the permanent winner. This pattern is neutral drift: chance competition among equivalent lineages.
scenes.visual: Hold the yellow base, then replay three miniature outcome strips beside the carried crypt with different winning colours. In every strip the teal pool bracket is unchanged while colour shares change. Merge the strips into one label: 'neutral drift'. Keep the grey differentiated stream moving upward.
scenes.narration: The number of supported positions stays roughly constrained while clone identities change. Balance belongs to the population, not every division. No cell is appointed the permanent winner. This pattern is neutral drift: chance competition among equivalent lineages.

scenes.tts: So follow descendants over time. During normal mouse-gut renewal, the pool can make specialized cells while most clones vanish and one may take over. The population persists even as its membership changes. A stable stem-cell pool persists while most of its clones vanish.
scenes.visual: Return attention to the large crypt. Let most starting colours disappear while one fills the base; keep the teal pool bracket and upward grey output. Then dim all labels except the final rule, preserving the moving crypt behind it.
scenes.narration: So follow descendants over time. During normal mouse-gut renewal, the pool can make specialized cells while most clones vanish and one may take over. The population persists even as its membership changes. A stable stem-cell pool persists while most of its clones vanish.

scenes.visual: End card over the still-living crypt: 'A stable stem-cell pool persists while most of its clones vanish.' Keep subtle upward cell motion and a gently breathing teal pool bracket until the cut.
